questions.q: What problem does partitioning FactOrders actually solve, at Lesson 8's 10-billion-row scale?
options: It splits one logical table into smaller physical chunks a query engine can read selectively, instead of one unmanageable block
It changes the fact table's grain from Lesson 8
It eliminates the need for dimension tables entirely
It converts the star schema into a snowflake schema
questions.explain: Lesson 8 fixed the logical shape; partitioning is about how that same table physically lives on disk at scale.

questions.q: Why does partitioning FactOrders by date usually beat partitioning by year or by second?
options: It matches the actual query pattern — small enough for pruning to help, large enough that each partition holds a real batch of data
Date partitioning is required by every query engine
Partitioning by year or second is always technically impossible
Date is the only column any fact table is allowed to partition on
questions.explain: DE Foundations Lesson 9's rule applies directly: pick a column you actually filter on often, with a manageable number of distinct values.

options: The query engine skipping entire partitions it can see don't match a filter, without opening a single file inside them
Deleting old partitions permanently to save storage
A process that only works on dimension tables, not fact tables
Compressing partition files to a smaller size
questions.explain: At scale, this is the difference between scanning the whole table and scanning only the partitions that could possibly match.

questions.q: Why is over-partitioning (e.g., partitioning by second) a real mistake, not just a harmless excess?
options: Pruning barely helps at that grain, and Databricks Lesson 23's small-files problem hits hard with thousands of tiny files to open
Over-partitioning always causes data corruption
It is impossible to over-partition a fact table
Over-partitioning only affects dimension tables
questions.explain: DE Foundations Lesson 9 called this a genuine mistake, and Databricks & Delta Lake Lesson 23's OPTIMIZE/ZORDER BY maintenance exists partly because of exactly this pattern.

questions.q: Why is under-partitioning (e.g., partitioning by year only) also a problem?
options: A query for a narrow date range like 'last week' still has to scan a whole year's worth of data, gaining nothing from pruning
Under-partitioning is technically impossible in Delta Lake
It only affects OLTP systems, never analytical fact tables
It requires more storage than any other partitioning scheme
questions.explain: Too few, oversized partitions mean pruning can't narrow a query down enough to matter.
